facts.statement: Deinosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 82 million years ago.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus is an extinct genus of eusuchian, either an alligatoroid crocodilian or a stem-group crocodilian, which lived during the Late Cretaceous around 82 million years ago

facts.statement: The largest known individuals of Deinosuchus surpassed 9 meters in total length.
facts.quote: with the largest surpassing 9 m in total length

facts.statement: Deinosuchus possessed large, robust teeth adapted for crushing.
facts.quote: It had large, robust teeth built for crushing

facts.quote: its back was covered with thick hemispherical osteoderms

facts.statement: Deinosuchus fossils have been found in 12 U.S. states, including Texas and Montana.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus fossils have been discovered in 12 U.S. states, including Texas, Montana, and many along the East Coast

facts.statement: Deinosuchus fossils have also been discovered in northern Mexico.
facts.quote: Fossils have also been found in northern Mexico

facts.statement: Deinosuchus was likely capable of killing and eating large dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus was probably capable of killing and eating large dinosaurs

facts.statement: A large tooth likely belonging to Deinosuchus was named Polydectes biturgidus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1869.
facts.quote: Another large tooth that likely came from Deinosuchus, discovered in Tar Heel sediments from neighboring Sampson County, was named Polydectes biturgidus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1869

facts.statement: Several fossil osteoderms were discovered at Willow Creek, Montana, in 1903.
facts.quote: In 1903, at Willow Creek, Montana, several fossil osteoderms were discovered

facts.statement: W. J. Holland assigned the Willow Creek specimens to the new species Deinosuchus hatcheri in 1909.
facts.quote: Holland assigned these specimens to a new genus and species, Deinosuchus hatcheri, in 1909

facts.statement: A 1940 expedition by the American Museum of Natural History found giant crocodilian fossils in Big Bend National Park, Texas.
facts.quote: A 1940 expedition by the American Museum of Natural History yielded more fossils of giant crocodilians, this time from Big Bend National Park in Texas

facts.statement: Specimens from Big Bend were described by Colbert and Bird in 1954 as Phobosuchus riograndensis.
facts.quote: These specimens were described by Edwin H. Colbert and Roland T. Bird in 1954, under the name Phobosuchus riograndensis

facts.statement: In 2024, a petition was submitted to the ICZN to replace the type species of Deinosuchus with Phobosuchus riograndensis.
facts.quote: In 2024, the replacement of the type species of Deinosuchus with Phobosuchus riograndensis has been petitioned to the ICZN

facts.statement: By 2002, David R. Schwimmer created a computer reconstruction of 90% of the Deinosuchus skull.
facts.quote: by 2002, David R. Schwimmer was able to create a composite computer reconstruction of 90% of the skull

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Walter and colleagues argues that many traits thought diagnostic for alligatoroids are actually more widespread.
facts.quote: In a 2025 study, Jules D. Walter and colleagues argue that many character states previously thought to be diagnostic for alligatoroids were actually much more widespread

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Cossette and Brochu classified D. rugosus as a nomen dubium due to insufficient diagnostic features.
facts.quote: In a 2020 study, Cossette and Brochu agreed that D. rugosus is dubious and undiagnostic, rendering it a nomen dubium

facts.statement: Cossette and Brochu named a new species, D. schwimmeri, for material from Appalachia previously assigned to D. rugosus.
facts.quote: and alternatively named a new species D. schwimmeri (named after fellow paleontologist David R. Schwimmer) from Appalachia

facts.statement: Deinosuchus possessed a broad, alligator-like snout with a slightly bulbous tip.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus had an alligator-like, broad snout, with a slightly bulbous tip.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Deinosuchus contained 23 teeth in each maxilla.
facts.quote: Each maxilla (the main tooth-bearing bone in the upper jaw) contained 23 teeth.

facts.statement: Each dentary bone in the lower jaw of Deinosuchus held at least 22 teeth.
facts.quote: The tooth count for each dentary (tooth-bearing bone in the lower jaw) was at least 22.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had thick, robust teeth adapted for crushing rather than piercing, with rear teeth being short, rounded, and blunt.
facts.quote: All the teeth were very thick and robust; those close to the rear of the jaws were short, rounded, and blunt. They appear to have been adapted for crushing, rather than piercing.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a unique skull shape not seen in other crocodilians, characterized by a broad skull inflated at the front around the nostrils.
facts.quote: The skull of Deinosuchus itself was of a unique shape not seen in any other living or extinct crocodilians; the skull was broad, but inflated at the front around the nares.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus possessed two unique holes in the premaxilla in front of the nostrils, though their function remains unknown.
facts.quote: Two holes in the premaxilla in front of the nares are present in this genus and are unique autapomorphies not seen in other crocodilians, but nothing is known at present regarding their function.

facts.statement: Estimates for the bite force of Deinosuchus range from 18,000 N to 102,803 N.
facts.quote: The bite force of Deinosuchus has been estimated to be 18000 N to 102803 N.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a secondary bony palate that allowed it to breathe through its nostrils while submerged.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus had a secondary bony palate, which would have permitted it to breathe through its nostrils while the rest of the head remained submerged underwater.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus vertebrae were procoelous, forming ball-and-socket joints with a concave front and convex rear.
facts.quote: The vertebrae were articulated in a procoelous manner, meaning they had a concave hollow on the front end and a convex bulge on the rear; these would have fit together to produce a ball and socket joint.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had unusually large, heavy, and deeply pitted osteoderms on its back, some roughly hemispherical in shape.
facts.quote: The osteoderms (scutes) covering the back of Deinosuchus were unusually large, heavy, and deeply pitted; some were of a roughly hemispherical shape.

facts.statement: The osteoderms and connective tissue of Deinosuchus acted as load-bearing reinforcement to support its massive body on land.
facts.quote: Together, the osteoderms and connective tissue would have served as load-bearing reinforcement to support the massive body of Deinosuchus out of water.

facts.statement: A 1954 reconstruction estimated Deinosuchus reached 15 meters in length based on a 1.5-meter skull and 1.8-meter lower jaw.
facts.quote: The original estimate from 1954 for the type specimen of the then-named "Phobosuchus riograndensis" were based on a skull of 1.5 m and a lower jaw of 1.8 m long, reconstructed with similar proportions to the Cuban crocodile giving a total estimated length of 15 m.

facts.statement: A 1999 estimate based on more complete remains placed Deinosuchus between 8 and 10 meters long and weighing 2.5 to 5 metric tons.
facts.quote: Using more complete remains, it was estimated in 1999 that the size attained by specimens of Deinosuchus varied from 8 to 10 m with weights from 2.5 to 5 MT.

facts.statement: A Texas specimen with a 1.31-meter skull suggested a total body length of 9.8 meters for Deinosuchus.
facts.quote: A reasonably well-preserved skull specimen discovered in Texas indicated the animal's head measured about 1.31 m, and its body length was estimated at 9.8 m.

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2002) suggested the largest D. riograndensis could reach 12 meters and weigh nearly 8.5 metric tons.
facts.quote: Schwimmer (2002) suggested the very largest individuals of D. riograndensis could reach sizes up to 12 m, 1.5 times that of the average D. rugosus, based on isometrically scaling vertebral lengths from the type specimens of "Phobosuchus riograndensis" (AMNH 3073) and Deinosuchus hatcheri, which he estimated would represent animals nearly 8.5 MT.

facts.statement: Iijima and Kubo (2020) estimated the type specimen AMNH 3073 measured between 7.37 and 8.17 meters long.
facts.quote: Iijima and Kubo (2020) estimated AMNH 3073 to measure 7.37 - 8.17 m in length using regression equations based on modern crocodilians, as the vertebrae of crocodilians scale with positive allometry.

facts.statement: A specimen with a 147.5 cm skull was estimated to reach a total length of 10.64 meters using American alligator regression equations.
facts.quote: A particularly large preserved skull from a D. riograndensis specimen was estimated to have come from an individual with a skull length of 147.5 cm. This length was used in conjunction with a regression equation relating skull length to total length in the American alligator to estimate a total length of 10.64 m for this particular specimen.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus has frequently been described as the largest crocodyliform in history.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus has often been described as the largest crocodyliform of all time.

facts.statement: Walter and colleagues (2025) argued previous size estimates were too high due to incorrect scaling, estimating maximum lengths of 10.5 m for D. riograndensis and 7.64 m for D. schwimmeri.
facts.quote: In their 2025 reclassification of Deinosuchus as a non-crocodylian eusuchian, Walter and colleagues stated that previous estimates may have overestimated its size as the genus has a relatively long snout, but these were based on taxa with shorter snouts such as the American alligator. The authors estimated the maximum total body length of D. riograndensis and D. schwimmeri at 10.5 m and 7.64 m respectively.

facts.statement: Walter and colleagues suggested a likely 95th percentile length of 7.66 m for D. riograndensis and 6.37 m for D. schwimmeri, with mean lengths of 5.8 m and 4.83 m respectively.
facts.quote: They suggested a 95 percentile body length estimate, which they considered more likely, of 7.66 m and 6.37 m respectively and a mean body length of 5.8 m and 4.83 m respectively, although the authors stated that D. riograndensis specimen AMNH 3073 would have been larger than the specimens used in the study.

facts.statement: Walter and colleagues suggested that Purussaurus was likely larger than Deinosuchus.
facts.quote: They also suggested that Purussaurus would have been larger than Deinosuchus.

facts.statement: Colbert and Bird (1954) speculated that Deinosuchus hunted and devoured dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In 1954, Edwin H. Colbert and Roland T. Bird speculated that Deinosuchus "may very well have hunted and devoured some of the dinosaurs with which it was contemporaneous".

facts.statement: Colbert (1961) confidently stated Deinosuchus hunted dinosaurs in the water where giant theropods could not reach.
facts.quote: Colbert restated this hypothesis more confidently in 1961: "Certainly this crocodile must have been a predator of dinosaurs; otherwise why would it have been so overwhelmingly gigantic? It hunted in the water where the giant theropods could not go."

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2002) noted hadrosaurid vertebrae with Deinosuchus tooth marks, supporting the idea it fed on dinosaurs.
facts.quote: David R. Schwimmer proposed in 2002 that several hadrosaurid tail vertebrae found near Big Bend National Park show evidence of Deinosuchus tooth marks, strengthening the hypothesis that Deinosuchus fed on dinosaurs in at least some instances.

facts.statement: Brochu (2003) agreed that Deinosuchus likely ate ornithopods occasionally.
facts.quote: In 2003, Christopher A. Brochu agreed that Deinosuchus "probably dined on ornithopods from time to time."

facts.statement: A 2014 study suggested Deinosuchus could perform a "death roll" similar to modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: A 2014 study suggested that it would have been able to perform a "death roll", like modern crocodiles.

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2010) noted a tyrannosauroid leg bone from the Ellisdale Fossil Site bore bite marks.
facts.quote: A 2010 review by Schwimmer noted NJSM 13096, a tyrannosauroid (either an immature Appalachiosaurus or a Dryptosaurus) leg bone in the collection of the New Jersey State Museum recovered from the Ellisdale Fossil Site had bite marks on it.

facts.statement: Schwimmer and Williams (1996) proposed Deinosuchus preyed on marine turtles.
facts.quote: Schwimmer and G. Dent Williams proposed in 1996 that Deinosuchus may have preyed on marine turtles.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus likely used its robust, flat rear teeth to crush turtle shells.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus would probably have used the robust, flat teeth near the back of its jaws to crush the turtle shells.

facts.statement: Shells of the sea turtle Bothremys found in Deinosuchus's eastern habitat bore bite marks likely made by the crocodilian.
facts.quote: The "side-necked" sea turtle Bothremys was especially common in the eastern habitat of Deinosuchus, and several of its shells have been found with bite marks that were most likely inflicted by the giant crocodilian.

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2002) concluded Deinosuchus feeding varied by location, with eastern North American specimens acting as opportunistic feeders like modern American alligators.
facts.quote: Schwimmer concluded in 2002 that the feeding patterns of Deinosuchus most likely varied by geographic location; the smaller Deinosuchus specimens of eastern North America would have been opportunistic feeders in an ecological niche similar to that of the modern American alligator.

facts.statement: Eastern North American Deinosuchus likely consumed marine turtles, large fish like Megalocoelacanthus, and smaller dinosaurs including young theropods.
facts.quote: They would have consumed marine turtles, large fish (such as Megalocoelacanthus), and smaller dinosaurs (including young theropods).

facts.statement: Larger Deinosuchus in Texas and Montana were likely specialized hunters of dinosaurs including hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, and theropods.
facts.quote: The bigger, but less common, Deinosuchus that lived in Texas and Montana might have been more specialized hunters, capturing and eating dinosaurs (such as hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, and small and large theropods).

facts.statement: Schwimmer noted no eastern theropods matched Deinosuchus's size, suggesting it was the apex predator in that region.
facts.quote: Schwimmer noted no theropod dinosaurs in Deinosuchus eastern range approached its size, indicating the massive crocodilian could have been the region's apex predator.

facts.statement: In 2002, Schwimmer debated whether Deinosuchus growth rings reflected annual periods, suggesting they could have been affected by migrations, climate, or ocean cycles.
facts.quote: Schwimmer noted in 2002 that Erickson and Brochu's assumptions about growth rates are only valid if the osteodermal rings reflect annual periods, as they do in modern crocodilians

facts.statement: The oldest Deinosuchus lived approximately 82 million years ago, and the youngest lived around 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest examples of this genus lived approximately 82 Ma, and the youngest lived around 73 Ma

facts.statement: Deinosuchus lived in North America, including present-day United States and northern Mexico, approximately 80 to 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Vivió en Norteamérica, lo que actualmente es Estados Unidos, y en lo que es el norte de México, hace aproximadamente entre 80 a 75 millones de años

facts.statement: Deinosuchus is among the largest crocodilians of all time, with length estimates ranging from 8 to 15 meters and a maximum estimated weight of 9 tons.
facts.quote: Se encuentra entre los mayores crocodilianos de todos los tiempos; las estimaciones sobre su longitud varían de 8 a 15 metros y un peso máximo estimado de 9 toneladas

facts.statement: In 1858, geologist Ebenezer Emmons described two large fossil teeth found in Bladen County, North Carolina.

facts.statement: A 1940 expedition from the American Museum of Natural History found more giant crocodilian fossils in Big Bend National Park, Texas.
facts.quote: Una expedición de 1940 del Museo Americano de Historia Natural halló más fósiles de crocodilianos gigantes, esta vez del Parque nacional Big Bend en Texas

facts.statement: Donald Baird and Jack Horner later assigned the Big Bend remains to Deinosuchus.

facts.statement: In the Aguja Formation of Texas, where some of the largest Deinosuchus specimens were found, these predators likely inhabited brackish-water bays.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus is an extinct genus of diapsid saurians belonging to the order Crocodilia and the superfamily Alligatoroidea.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus (gr. "cocodrilo terrible") es un género extinto de saurópsidos (reptiles) diápsidos del orden Crocodilia y pertenecientes a la superfamilia Alligatoroidea

facts.statement: The name Deinosuchus derives from the Greek words deinos, meaning "terrible", and suchos, meaning "crocodile".
facts.quote: Deinosuchus deriva del griego δεινός/deinos, que significa "terrible", y σοῦχος/suchos, que significa "cocodrilo"

facts.statement: The maximum estimated size of Deinosuchus is between 9 and 10 meters.
facts.quote: El tamaño máximo alcanzado por Deinosuchus ha sido estimado entre 9 e 10 metros.

facts.statement: Gregory M. Erickson and Christopher A. Brochu estimated the size to be between 8 and 10 meters in 1999.
facts.quote: Una estimación mucho más baja - de 8 a 10 metros — fue dada por Gregory M. Erickson y Christopher A. Brochu en 1999.

facts.statement: In 2002, David R. Schwimmer noted that the smallest and most widespread form of Deinosuchus in eastern North America usually had skulls about 1 meter long.
facts.quote: David R. Schwimmer notó en 2002 que la forma más pequeña y difundida de Deinosuchus hallada en el este de Norteamérica usualmente tenía cráneos de cerca de 1 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Schwimmer estimates that the largest specimens had a total body length of over 12 meters and possibly weighed 8.5 tons or more.
facts.quote: Schwimmer estima que los mayores especímenes tenían una longitud corporal total de más de 12 metros, y quizás pesaban unas 8.5 toneladas o más.

facts.statement: A well-preserved skull found in Texas measured about 1.31 meters, leading Schwimmer to calculate a body length of 9.8 meters.
facts.quote: Un cráneo razonablemente bien preservado descubierto en Texas indica que la cabeza del animal medía cerca de 1.31 metros, y a partir de este Schwimmer calculó una longitud corporal de 9.8 metros.

facts.statement: Fossils of this large alligatoroid have been found in ten US states and northern Mexico.
facts.quote: Fósiles de este gran aligatoroide se han descubierto en diez estados de EE. UU., además del norte de México.

facts.statement: All known specimens of Deinosuchus were found in rocks dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Todos los especímenes conocidos de Deinosuchus fueron hallados en rocas que datan de la época del Campaniense del período Cretácico Superior.

facts.statement: The oldest specimens of the genus lived approximately 80 million years ago, and the most recent about 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Los más antiguos ejemplares del género vivieron hace aproximadamente 80 millones de años, y los más recientes hace unos 73 millones de años.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus was present on both sides of the Niobrara Sea.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus estaba presente a ambos lados del Mar de Niobrara.

facts.statement: The distribution of specimens suggests that these giant crocodilians may have preferred estuarine environments.
facts.quote: La distribución de los especímenes de Deinosuchus indica que estos crocodilianos gigantescos pueden haber preferido ambientes de estuarios.

facts.statement: Schwimmer noted that no theropod dinosaurs of comparable size are known from the eastern range of Deinosuchus, indicating it may have been the apex predator of the region.
facts.quote: Schwimmer señaló que no se conocen dinosaurios terópodos en el rango oriental de Deinosuchus que se aproximen a su tamaño, indicando que el gran crocodiliano pudo haber sido el superdepredador de la región.

facts.statement: A 1999 study by Gregory M. Erickson and Christopher A. Brochu suggested that Deinosuchus had a growth rate comparable to modern crocodilians but maintained over a longer period.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 1999 realizado por Gregory M. Erickson y Christopher A. Brochu sugirió que la tasa de crecimiento de Deinosuchus era comparable a la de los crocodilianos modernos, pero se mantenía a lo largo de un período más largo.

facts.statement: Based on growth rings in dorsal osteoderms, estimates indicate it may have taken Deinosuchus nearly 35 years to reach full adult size, with some individuals living over 50 years.
facts.quote: Sus estimaciones, basadas en los anillos de crecimiento de los osteodermos dorsales de varios especímenes, indican que le pudo haber llevado a un Deinosuchus cerca de 35 años alcanzar su tamaño adulto completo, y que los individuos más viejos pueden haber vivido por más de 50 años.

facts.statement: While often described as the largest crocodilian of all time, some other crocodiliforms including Purussaurus, Rhamphosuchus, and Sarcosuchus may have equaled or exceeded its size.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus ha sido frecuentemente descrito como el mayor crocodiliano de todos los tiempos, pero algunos otros crocodiliformes - incluyendo a Purussaurus, Rhamphosuchus y Sarcosuchus — pueden haberlo igualado o excedido en tamaño.

facts.statement: Despite some disagreement over its exact size, fossil remains indicate Deinosuchus was substantially larger than any modern crocodilian.
facts.quote: Aunque existe cierto disentimiento sobre su tamaño exacto, los restos fósiles son aun así suficientes para indicar que Deinosuchus era sustancialmente mayor que cualquier crocodiliano moderno.
